title: First Fridays
hook: nine first Fridays of confession and communion, from the Sacred Heart devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday, three o'clock: the ninth hour, an hour of prayer that became the hour Jesus died. Your line was the hour of mercy. Where were you when three came around? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

A parish bulletin, near the bottom, between the bake sale and a reminder about parking: First Friday. Confessions before the morning Mass. Adoration afterward. Some people circle it. Some keep a small card in a wallet with boxes to tick, month after month, until the boxes run out. It's a devotion with a number built into it, and a promise attached to the number. Today's word is the name for that circled date.
screen: `FIRST FRIDAY: CONFESSIONS, MASS.` → `BOXES TO TICK.` → `A NUMBER AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: It begins in a convent in France, with a nun this path has met before, Margaret Mary Alacoque. In her account, Jesus showed her his heart and asked that people receive communion on the first Friday of each month, in reparation: making up, in love, for the coldness his love so often meets. Why Friday? Because the Gospels place the crucifixion on the day of preparation before the Sabbath, the day Christians call Friday. Every Friday echoes Good Friday, and the first one of each month became a small Good Friday on the calendar. Next, the promise. In a letter, Margaret Mary passed on what's known as the great promise: that those who received communion on the first Friday for nine months in a row would not die without the grace of repentance and the sacraments. That's where the nine comes from. The Church has permitted the devotion and encouraged it. It doesn't teach that nine Fridays work like a ticket; in Catholic teaching, grace is never bought by keeping a schedule. Third, what the day actually holds. The devotion asks for communion, and the Church asks anyone aware of serious sin to go to confession before communion. That's why parishes open the confessional on a first Friday morning. Some add an hour of adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, or a litany of the Sacred Heart. Last, the heart behind it. In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." A first Friday is an appointment with that invitation. Nine of them, one a month, is a long time to keep showing up. That's part of the point.
screen: `MARGARET MARY: COMMUNION, IN REPARATION.` · `FRIDAY ECHOES GOOD FRIDAY.` · `NINE IN A ROW: THE GREAT PROMISE.` · `CONFESSION, COMMUNION, ADORATION.` · then, large: `I WILL REFRESH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the next first Friday. Sit back, and let the noise of the day thin out. Find, in your head or on your phone, the first Friday of next month. Just mark it: a dot, a star, a single word. Then sit with what that day might hold. If you're Catholic and you pray, you can plan to go to Mass that morning, or to confession, or simply to stop into a church for a few minutes. If that isn't your practice, the day can still carry something: an hour kept free, one kindness for someone who's worn out. Then let the plans go, and rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
First Fridays. The first Friday of each month, kept with communion in honor of the Sacred Heart, and, in Margaret Mary's account, kept nine months in a row with a promise attached. Today's word.
Your line: nine fridays. Today, find out when your nearest parish holds its first Friday Mass or confessions, and keep the time somewhere you'll see it. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep the First Friday devotion go to Mass and receive communion on the first Friday of the month, often after confession, in honor of the Sacred Heart; some keep nine in a row, and parishes often add confessions and adoration that day.

fork.setup: you're a sister in Margaret Mary's convent, and she tells you what she says Jesus asked for on the first Friday of each month. what was it?
options: a fast from all food that day.
communion, in reparation for coldness toward his love.
fork.reveal: communion, in reparation: making up in love for the coldness his love meets. the great promise of the nine Fridays was passed on in one of her letters.

trapdoor: what you thought: first Friday is a parish scheduling thing.
what it means: a monthly day of communion in reparation to the Sacred Heart, kept nine months running with a promise attached.
what a scholar hears: the great promise comes from a letter of Margaret Mary Alacoque; the Church permits and encourages the devotion without teaching that it guarantees salvation.

sources.quoted: Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

sources.ref: Margaret Mary Alacoque, Autobiography and Letters (the first Friday request and the great promise)

notes: The 'great promise' (communion on nine consecutive first Fridays; not dying in disgrace or without the sacraments, with final repentance) is paraphrased from Margaret Mary's letter as commonly summarized; confirm the wording and that the letter is the right source.
'The Church has permitted the devotion and encouraged it' and 'doesn't teach that nine Fridays work like a ticket' are general summaries of Church practice and theology; confirm.
CCC 1385 (confession before communion for anyone conscious of grave sin) paraphrased.
Friday as the day of the crucifixion: the Gospels say the day of preparation before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42, John 19:31, 42); stated as 'the day Christians call Friday'.
Day 673 covered the Sacred Heart feast and Margaret Mary's visions; this day keeps to the First Friday practice.
